04 · Read & review

The transcript

0:00 / 0:00

Submit all six answers to unlock the transcript. You can then listen and read together.

The clearer 2012 transfer schedule appeared at first to resolve the uncertainty surrounding the missing authorisation register. It identified an external records company, a box reference and a date designated for collection. Fiona Bell nevertheless cautioned that the document was the trust's own schedule, not a receipt issued by a storage provider.

Emma examined the distinction before discussing the news with Sarah. An organisation might prepare a box for transfer, record its departure and then assume that it had arrived safely. Each proposition required a different evidential basis. The schedule substantiated preparation; its remaining marks needed interpretation.

The named storage contractor had since changed its trading name. A public notice supported continuity between the old and new names, but established neither the custody of this particular box nor its survival.

“Surely we can ask them directly,” Sarah said.

“Fiona should,” Emma replied. “The trust is the customer, and the records may contain former applicants' personal information. We're not entitled to their contents simply because they might be relevant.”

A tick appeared in the schedule's Collected column beside the box reference. Sarah treated it as evidence that a driver had taken possession. Emma regarded it more cautiously. The mark had no visible signature; the person who made it and the event it represented were unknown. It could have been added before collection, during a stock check or afterwards.

Fiona contacted the successor storage company. Staff agreed to review its historic indexing records, but initially found no signed acknowledgement of receipt. They undertook to communicate with the trust rather than disclose client material directly to Emma.

Helen Ward's reply arrived while Emma was comparing the two records systems. Her cousin had not located any surviving bank paperwork confirming payment of the selected grant. The absence was unsurprising after fifteen years and supplied no reason to associate the family's application with the missing authorisation register. Emma noted the limitation and did not press Helen for another disclosure.

Later Fiona forwarded a brief description from the storage company's internal index. The box number appeared beside the words Location changed. There was no contents list, no explanation of the previous location and no indication of who had amended the entry.

Sarah thought the notation meant the box must once have been in the warehouse. That was plausible, Emma conceded, but not established. The same reference might have been transferred from a predecessor system, corrected during data migration or linked to a physical box that could not yet be identified. She would not convert the mere existence of a catalogue entry into an uninterrupted chain of custody.

On a fresh page she separated the stages: Prepared for collection, Marked collected, Received by contractor, Moved internally. She placed the available document beside each and left the unverified stages blank.

There was an irony in the investigation. Emma had been trying to determine whether authorisation entries corresponded to completed financial transfers. Now she was asking whether an administrative transfer entry corresponded to the physical movement of a box. In both cases, a record of intention or approval was not interchangeable with a verified outcome.

She asked Fiona to enquire what the index had meant by Location changed: the former location, the destination and the date of amendment. A detailed answer might lead to the register. It might equally reveal a clerical correction.

Either result would be better than an accusation built on an unexplained tick.
